source.title: The Curse of Precision: A Data Scaling Law for High-Precision Robotic Manipulation
source.authors: Cui-Jie Xu; Yuan-Fan Xu; Min Xue; Jian-Jie Lin; Jian Wang; Xu-Dong Zhang; Yu Wang; Jin-Cheng Yu

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; minor line-wrap and extraction artifacts do not prevent reading.
record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling relationships in robotic imitation learning, an embodied task and training regime beyond language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The paper cites language-model scaling laws as background, but its own experiments concern robotic manipulation, demonstration counts, success rates, and task precision. It does not measure language-model loss, parameter/token/compute scaling, downstream language-model performance, or compute-optimal allocation.
record.test_reason: The study directly tests V5 in simulated robotic behavior cloning: failure rate versus demonstration count is fitted to a power law, including a capacity condition where that relationship fails.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors report failure-rate power laws and a separate precision law, interpret its fitted limit c as a system-capability metric, and identify sufficient model capacity as a prerequisite in Roll Ball. Their proposed precision limit and diagnostic applications remain based on simulated behavior-cloning fits.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses behavior cloning with Diffusion Policy in simulated robotic tasks and measures success rate and task precision versus demonstration volume; it does not use language-model pretraining or held-out cross-entropy.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scaling behavior depends on denoiser capacity. The limit precision c also changes with observation modality, expert strategy, and domain randomization.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed target success rate, inferred demonstration requirements fit log(N)=m/(P−c)+n across task tolerances.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In these simulated behavior-cloning tasks, data requirements grow as exp(m/(P−c)+n) as tolerance approaches a fitted limit c.

fits_no_version.finding: The fitted precision limit changes from 2.35 mm to 1.27 mm with a different expert, 3.85 mm without a wrist camera, and 1.00 mm with less randomization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The fitted precision asymptote in robotic behavior cloning depends on sensing, demonstration strategy, and task variation.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA) 2026; accepted for ICRA 2026
record.problems: Experiments are all in simulation and use behavior cloning. Each (N, P) data point corresponds to a single training run. The paper reports confidence intervals for SR estimates, but no uncertainty estimates for the fitted scaling-law parameters.
record.rows_left_out: No reported scaling results relevant to V5 were left out. Table III's R2 values for the three target SRs are included in the notes accompanying T3-01–T3-04 rather than separate rows.

untested.parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute over several orders of magnitude.
Independent validation that fits from small runs predict loss in runs orders of magnitude larger; interpolation or extrapolation used to construct precision curves does not establish this.
Loss-minimising parameter and token allocations under fixed compute budgets.
Architecture effects at fixed parameter count; the capacity comparison changes model size.
Other modalities and training regimes beyond these three simulated behavior-cloning tasks; parameter and compute scaling, physical-robot validation, and broad scaling ranges are not established.
Downstream performance as a function of upstream pretraining scale or loss; these are direct evaluations of the trained robotic policies.
Sensitivity of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations to setup and fitting choices, disagreements between published laws, and bending of an otherwise established scaling curve.

record.verdict_notes: All tabulated numerical values match the supplied text. Each (N,P) point uses one training run; reported SR averages the three best evaluations during training. Evaluation intervals do not quantify training-run variability or fitted-parameter uncertainty. Precision-law points are derived from the success-rate fits, and a shared c across target success rates is enforced during fitting. Those results therefore provide neither independent large-run extrapolation validation nor additional evidence for the same power-law form.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small language-model runs predict much larger runs.
Effects of language-model depth, width, and architecture on held-out loss.

The study tests scaling in robotic imitation learning only; it does not test image/video foundation models, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer, or whether language-model held-out loss follows the same form.
Downstream-task performance and its relationship to language-model pretraining loss or scale.
Dependence of language-model exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices, and disagreement among published language-model laws.

rows.subject: Diffusion Policy — Roll Ball, standard-capacity denoiser
rows.operation_detail: Compare the failure-rate scaling fit at standard denoiser capacity.
rows.measure: R2 for success-rate scaling law
rows.note: The text says a clear scaling law failed to emerge and success did not improve predictably with more data.
rows.check: Valid scaling result, not merely a method-performance comparator: the authors explicitly report failure of predictable data scaling at this capacity.

rows.subject: Diffusion Policy — Roll Ball, high-capacity denoiser
rows.operation_detail: Compare the failure-rate scaling fit after increasing denoiser capacity.
rows.measure: R2 for success-rate scaling law
rows.note: The text says a distinct scaling law appeared after denoiser capacity was substantially increased.
rows.check: Valid scaling result: increasing capacity restores the reported power-law relationship.
